titre: The “Seventh Continent” Is Not an Island
accroche: We imagine it as an island of waste visible from space. In reality you can cross it by boat without seeing anything
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1997, the sailor and researcher Charles Moore returns from the Los Angeles-to-Hawaii transpacific race by crossing the North Pacific subtropical gyre, an area few boats use because it offers neither favorable wind nor commercial interest. He would later write, in an essay published in 2003: “As I gazed from the deck at the surface of what ought to have been a pristine ocean, I was confronted, as far as the eye could see, with the sight of plastic.” Expecting a pristine ocean, he found nothing but plastic as far as the eye could see.

## What the Account Wrongly Suggests

This testimony, widely repeated since, fed the image of a “seventh continent”: a mass of waste so dense that one could almost walk on it, visible from a plane or a satellite. This image is false, and the agencies that study the area say so explicitly. NOAA compares the reality to grains of pepper scattered in a bowl of soup rather than to an island: you can sail through the heart of the concentration zone without seeing any waste with the naked eye, and “the area richest in plastic is a thousand miles from land, and you can't see it from space or from an airplane.”

The zone itself results from a well-identified physical phenomenon: four clockwise-turning currents encircle the North Pacific and form a gyre, a vast ocean whirlpool that slowly gathers, at its center, everything that floats and does not degrade quickly, first and foremost plastic.

## What the Numbers Show, Up Close

A study published in 2018 in *Scientific Reports*, based on aerial measurements and net tows covering the zone, estimates its surface at about 1.6 million km², for about 79,000 tons of plastic spread across 1,800 billion fragments. The detail of this figure shifts common sense as much as Moore's account did: microplastics under 5 millimeters make up 94% of the total number of fragments, but only 8% of the total mass. The rest of the mass, the bulk of what could physically be collected, comes from larger objects, first and foremost fishing nets and gear lost or abandoned at sea.

The correction therefore does not lighten the problem, it shifts it. This is not an island that could be encircled and cleaned up in one sweep: it is a cloud of mostly invisible fragments, mixed with fishing gear that keeps on trapping marine wildlife years after being lost. The “continent” we imagine as solid would, paradoxically, be easier to deal with than what actually exists.

carte.punch: The plastic “seventh continent” is not an island: you can cross it without seeing anything.
carte.idee: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch is neither solid nor visible from space. According to a 2018 study, 94% of its 1,800 billion fragments are microplastics under 5 mm, but they weigh only 8% of its total mass, the rest coming mostly from lost fishing gear.

quiz.question: Why can't the plastic “seventh continent” be seen from a plane or from space?
choix: Because most of its fragments are millimeter-sized and scattered, not a solid mass
Because it has been largely cleaned up since its discovery in the 1990s
Because it moves too fast to be photographed
quiz.explication: 94% of the fragments that make up the zone are microplastics under 5 mm, scattered over more than a million km², nothing like a solid, identifiable mass. The cleanup remains very partial, and the zone's drift speed has nothing to do with its low visibility, which comes solely from the dispersal of the fragments.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does the North Pacific plastic concentration zone physically come from?
choix: From a continuous leak from a plastics factory on a Pacific island
From four clockwise-turning currents that encircle the North Pacific and form a gyre
From a single cargo ship that lost its entire plastic load in 1997
From an underwater volcanic phenomenon that would produce plastic debris
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The zone results from four clockwise-turning currents that encircle the North Pacific and form a gyre, a whirlpool that slowly gathers whatever floats without degrading.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the 2018 study in Scientific Reports, what makes up the bulk of the zone's plastic mass, once the microplastics are set aside?
choix: Plastic bottles thrown overboard by cruise ship passengers
Food packaging coming directly from the American coasts
Debris from shipping containers sunk in storms
Fishing nets and gear lost or abandoned at sea
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Microplastics make up only 8% of the total mass despite 94% of the fragments: the bulk of the mass comes from larger objects, first and foremost lost fishing nets and gear.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Charles Moore say he discovered when crossing the North Pacific gyre in 1997?
choix: A pristine ocean, exactly as he expected
A solid island of waste, visible from the deck of his boat
Plastic as far as the eye could see, when he expected a pristine ocean
A school of dead fish, poisoned by chemical discharges
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Moore says that, expecting a pristine ocean, he found nothing but plastic as far as the eye could see, an account since repeated to feed the mistaken image of a “seventh continent.”
